new_statements.quote: Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable in Hunjara and Kaina Ke.
new_statements.citation: Gray, Rachel, Rachel Hiley & Thom Retsema. 2015. The Sociolinguistic Situation of the Hunjara-Kaina Ke [hkk] Language, Oro Province, Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2015-027. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 7.1.1 Phonology, subhead 'Stress', printed p.35 (PDF p.40)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (78 pp., SIL ESR 2015-027, title page reads "The Sociolinguistic Situation of the Hunjara-Kaina Ke [hkk] Language, Oro Province, Papua New Guinea"). extracted text of PDF p.40 (printed p.35), sec. 7.1.1 Phonology, subhead "Stress", gives exactly: "Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable in Hunjara and Kaina Ke." One sentence, no examples, between the vowel discussion (7.1.1.2) and "Current trial orthography"; the phonology section is first-hand from the team's 2006 wordlist elicitation (sec. 7.1.1.1: "The following consonant phones were recorded during wordlist elicitation sessions") plus the 2004 ADW worksheet. Identity: the report is explicitly about hkk, both varieties…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, in both the Hunjara and the Kaina Ke varieties. Corroborated independently by Smallhorn 2011:80 (PL 625), who lists Hunjara among the Binanderean languages exhibiting penultimate stress on the basis of her own stress-marked Hunjara wordlist (168 marked entries, all penultimate, e.g. a'visa, hom'boru, ambu'reri). Note the contrast with Orokaiva proper, for which Larsen & Larsen 1977:12 report fixed initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None given; 'typically' implies some, unstated. Smallhorn 2011:80 adds that verbs in Binanderean daughter languages (Binandere, Korafe) follow a different rule (stress on the first syllable of the tense/person suffix), but gives no Hunjara verb data on that point; her penultimate claim is explicitly 'at least in the case of non-verbs'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from survey wordlist elicitation (SIL-PNG 170-word list + 20 phrases, 11 villages: Ombisusu, Sairope, Sirorata, Papaki, Ilimo, Sauni for Hunjara; Waju, Perive, Sengi, Kokoda Village, Amada for Kaina Ke). Source is an SIL sociolinguistic survey report whose sec. 7.1.1 is a short first-hand phonology sketch (consonant and vowel charts, stress, orthography); Glottolog types it wordlist/socling. Not a dedicated phonology; no examples or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Gray et al. 2015 covers both named varieties of hkk, Hunjara (Ke) and Kaina Ke (the Kokoda-area variety with th/θ), and states the same penultimate rule for both; both are hunj1241 (no separate glottocodes). Smallhorn 2011's corroborating data are Hunjara Ke (informant in Australia). The source the earlier scan named, Larsen & Larsen 1977, describes Orokaiva proper (orok1269 [okv], Agenehambo-Wasida dialect) and reports INITIAL stress; it is not a description of hkk and must not be attached to this entry.

sources.note: Sec. 7.1.1 Phonology, subhead 'Stress', printed p.35 (PDF p.40): 'Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable in Hunjara and Kaina Ke.' One sentence, no examples; based on the team's 11 village wordlists (170 words + 20 phrases, elicited by Retsema 2006) and the 2004 Alphabet Design Workshop worksheet. Wordlists in App. C are not stress-marked.

sources.citation: Smallhorn, Jacinta. 2011. The Binanderean languages of Papua New Guinea: reconstruction and subgrouping. Pacific Linguistics 625. Canberra: ANU. (open access, ANU Open Research)
sources.note: Sec. 3.6 'tone and stress', printed p.80 (PDF p.96): 'penultimate stress is assumed for two- and three-syllable words (at least in the case of non-verbs), based on the analyses of stress in the present-day languages; Suena, Zia, Binandere, Hunjara, Tafota Baruga, and Korafe all exhibit this pattern.' Hunjara data are the author's own (informant in Australia, 'Smallhorn 2007' unpublished wordlist, siglum JS07); the data appendix marks stress on 168 of 424 Hunjara entries, penultimate throughout (a'visa 'ashes', ko'ropa 'black palm', hom'boru 'cassowary', iŋ'gose 'embers/black', ambu'reri 'dead…

sources.citation: Larsen, Robert & Marlys Larsen. 1977. Orokaiva phonology and orthography. In R. Loving (ed.), Phonologies of five P.N.G. languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 19), 5-28. Ukarumpa: SIL.
sources.note: NOT hkk: describes the Orokaiva-proper dialect 'between Agenehambo and Wasida on the road from Popondetta to Kokoda' (p.5); no mention of Hunjara. Sec. 5.1 p.12: 'Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word' -- INITIAL, i.e. a different rule from the penultimate one reported for Hunjara. The earlier world scan named this work for hkk; it should not be used for hkk.
